items.title: Captured Federal Court Approves Iowa Toxic Lead Detonation Sought by Trump
items.author: Lisa Graves
items.content:
Today, the Trump administration plans to detonate 9,500 pounds of lead azide, a weapons-grade compound of lead and nitrogen used in bombs. The Army’s destruction of 68 barrels of this toxic substance is expected to release a 100-mile plume of dust that could deposit lead in communities across Iowa and neighboring states, contaminating water, farmland, and more. Lead is a neurotoxin that can cause brain damage. There is no safe level of exposure, and it does not break down in soil.

Earlier this week, Trump absurdly tried to blame Iowa’s incoming Democratic governor, Rob Sand, for any harm caused by the lead-filled barrels, even though he has not even taken office yet. Governor-elect Sand has urged the federal government to give Iowans more information about the planned detonation.

The situation began earlier this year, in March, when the Army found signs that some of the barrels it had stored for decades at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, had degraded into a crystalline form that could result in spontaneous detonation.

In response, the government issued a contract this spring to MuniRem Environmental, a company specializing in chemical mitigation, to help neutralize the lead azide barrels, a process it has successfully done before. Despite the lower cost and much smaller risk of explosive consequences, the government reportedly canceled that contract in May–abruptly–opting instead to proceed with its own plan of blowing up the barrels. When MuniRem raised concerns with the EPA about the potential dangers of detonating the lead, it received no reply.

The Trump administration is invoking an emergency exception to environmental rules to justify the detonation, while planning to filter the resulting plume of gas and dousing it with water. The government asserts that temperature changes, like the coming winter season, could result in unmitigated explosions of the lead barrels if it does not blow them up first.

Local and national environmental groups sued to stop Trump’s plan, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit temporarily halted the detonation a few days ago. On Monday night, however, a three-judge panel approved the plans, ruling that the administration could detonate the barrels, a procedure it asserted was safer than allowing them to continue to degrade.

On the surface, this is a unanimous ruling, which makes it seems as though the law compelled the result. But we’re talking about the most captured federal court in the country, rivaling even the U.S. Supreme Court. Ten of the eleven judges on the court, which covers the Dakotas and Minnesota straight down to Arkansas, were appointed by Republican presidents.

Only one judge on the entire court was appointed by a Democratic president: Jane Kelly of Iowa, who was nominated by President Obama in 2013. Due to the random process for judges getting assigned to three-judge panels, she was not selected to hear this appeal. We do not know how she would have ruled, but the packing of this circuit court means that there is zero chance of any party drawing a panel with a majority of Democrat-appointed judges.

Statistically, the chance of drawing an all Republican-appointed panel on that circuit is nearly 75%. The chance of having a majority of Republican-appointed judges hear your appeal is 100%, just like with the U.S. Supreme Court, where six of the nine justices are Republican appointees.

The Circuit’s lead detonation ruling is unsigned, leaving its author anonymous. Two of the judges siding with Trump, however, were hand-picked by him for their positions of power.

Justin Smith was confirmed in June by Senate Republicans 48-43, with all Democrats voting no. Smith, who was born in 1985, could remain on the federal bench for another 40 years or more.

Before becoming a judge, he was a partner at the law firm founded by John Sauer. Sauer argued for immunity from criminal prosecution for Trump while he and Smith were partners and co-owners at the James Otis Law Group. Trump praised Smith’s role in that litigation, in which the Supreme Court, led by John Roberts, invented presidential immunity from criminal prosecution. Trump said Justin “played a BIG role in securing a Supreme Court Landmark Victory on Presidential Immunity.”

Sauer was named Solicitor General and Smith got rewarded with a federal judgeship.

Numerous civil rights groups opposed Smith’s confirmation. He has actively attacked abortion access and trans rights. He is also part of what I call Leonard Leo’s Missouri Posse: a group of lawyers tied to the right-wing agenda and money directed by Leo, to whom Trump delegated the selection of Supreme Court candidates during his first term.

I don’t think there was any chance that environmental groups and Iowa community members suing to stop or further delay the lead detonation would get a fair hearing from Smith.

Another Trump appointee on the panel was Steven Grasz. When he was nominated to become a federal judge, the American Bar Association gave him the worst possible rating: unanimously Not Qualified (NQ). The ABA concluded that Grasz could not be trusted with a judgeship “because of judicial temperament concerns, specifically ‘lack of open-mindedness and freedom from bias.’”

Grasz is a long-time activist against abortion access and the separation of church and state. He has repeatedly attacked LGBTQ rights and supported conversion therapy, a cruel practice that has been condemned by mainstream psychologists.

The Republican-controlled Senate confirmed him in 2017 anyway, by a 50-48 vote, with every Democrat voting against his confirmation.

The third judge on the panel was Bobby Shepherd, who was appointed to the Eighth Circuit by George W. Bush in 2006. Shepherd has since joined numerous controversial rulings, including blocking President Biden’s student loan debt relief plan. Unfortunately, the Roberts Court sided with Schmitt, despite Missouri’s obvious lack of standing to challenge the Democratic plan to give debt relief to Missourians and other Americans.

Earlier this year, the Eighth Circuit also sided with the Trump administration against Minnesota as the state tried to stop Trump’s violent siege of Minneapolis. That federal operation resulted in deaths and injuries, including what I consider to be the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by ICE agents, and the seizure of numerous immigrants who committed no crimes.

This is a circuit court where Republican appointees have routinely chosen to retire when a Republican is president, locking in Republican control. Meanwhile, Democratic appointees–like the first woman and first Black man on the court–stayed on as they aged only for Republicans to flip their seats, as happened with Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

The Eighth Circuit is a cautionary tale of court capture by right-wing special interests, resulting in a court predisposed to side with Trump and against ordinary people.

It is one of the reasons why I support term limits across the federal judiciary, not just for the Supreme Court, among other needed reforms.

The right-wing court capture scheme has already broken so many of our rights, and now it seems its appointees are willing to let Iowa and surrounding areas be poisoned, too.
